clinicalPearls: Regarded as generalised pustular psoriasis presenting in pregnancy; the historical name impetigo herpetiformis is a misnomer as it is neither infective nor herpetic.
Typically presents in the third trimester with erythematous patches fringed by sterile subcorneal pustules that extend centrifugally, often starting in the flexures.
Systemic upset is characteristic, with fever, malaise, delirium, and features of hypocalcaemia such as tetany, and it can be life-threatening.
Unlike the other pregnancy dermatoses it is often not markedly itchy; pain, burning and systemic illness dominate.
Hypocalcaemia, hypoalbuminaemia and secondary hypoparathyroidism may occur and require correction.
It carries a genuine risk of placental insufficiency, stillbirth and neonatal death, so fetal surveillance is essential.
First-line treatment is systemic corticosteroid; ciclosporin is an option in resistant disease and delivery may be needed if the fetus is compromised at term.
It tends to recur in subsequent pregnancies, often with earlier onset and greater severity.
reference.pathophysiology: Pustular psoriasis of pregnancy is a variant of generalised pustular psoriasis in which the pregnant state acts as a trigger, and a subset of patients carry mutations in IL36RN encoding the interleukin-36 receptor antagonist, leading to unopposed interleukin-36 signalling and intense neutrophilic inflammation. This produces the characteristic sterile spongiform pustules of Kogoj within the epidermis. Contributory factors include the relative hypocalcaemia and reduced parathyroid hormone activity of pregnancy and possible hormonal influences. The neutrophil-rich sterile pustulation and systemic inflammatory response account for the fever, leucocytosis and constitutional illness, while placental dysfunction underlies the associated fetal risk.
additionalDifferentials: generalised pustular psoriasis unrelated to pregnancy
widespread bacterial or candidal pustular infection
additionalInvestigations: skin biopsy (spongiform pustules of Kogoj, parakeratosis and neutrophilic infiltrate)
serum calcium, albumin, phosphate and parathyroid hormone
full blood count and inflammatory markers (leucocytosis, raised C-reactive protein and ESR)
swabs and pustule culture to confirm sterility and exclude infection
fetal surveillance with cardiotocography and growth ultrasound; consider IL36RN genetic testing
redFlags: high fever, rigors, delirium or haemodynamic instability indicating systemic sepsis-like decompensation
tetany, perioral or peripheral paraesthesiae or seizures from hypocalcaemia
reduced fetal movements, growth restriction or abnormal cardiotocography signalling placental insufficiency
rapidly extending confluent pustulation with skin failure and fluid or electrolyte loss
signs of secondary bacterial infection or septicaemia
reference.prognosis: With prompt systemic treatment, correction of electrolyte disturbance and fetal monitoring, maternal outcome is usually good, but there is a real risk of stillbirth, fetal growth restriction and neonatal death from placental insufficiency. It characteristically recurs in later pregnancies, frequently earlier and more severely.
pitfalls: Mistaking sterile pustules for infection and delaying corticosteroid while pursuing antibiotics.
Failing to measure and correct calcium, risking tetany and seizures from unrecognised hypocalcaemia.
Underestimating fetal risk and omitting fetal surveillance, missing placental insufficiency.
Attributing the eruption to a benign pregnancy dermatosis and undertreating a potentially fatal condition.
Abruptly stopping systemic corticosteroid after delivery, precipitating a rebound flare.
